rv.q: There is much to admire here, as well as much that needs trimming.
The Last Ship is an awesome spectacle and a heartfelt one too.
The Last Ship ends up as an engaging depiction of a community in crisis.

As it briefly docks at Theatre Royal Drury Lane, with Sting himself in a lead role, it’s worth saluting the venture (and applauding its decent tunes), but it lacks a sufficient feel-good factor and goes overboard in its scale.
The Last Ship is earnest and well-meaning with some good songs, but it simply doesn’t float.
It has a great deal going for it and is far from a mere vanity project for a man who has achieved greatness many times over in a successful career spanning close to 50 years.
Visually stunning, musically rich and anchored by a palpable sense of community, it offers plenty to admire even when the storytelling occasionally struggles under the weight of its own ambitions.
Sting gives a spirited performance as the illness-riddled foreman Jackie White, bringing his real-life experience living in Wallsend and landing the show some-much needed heart.
It all makes for an evening that is not without its delights, the spectacular set first and foremost and the score never less than pleasing.
Heartfelt and quirky in equal measure, but the holes in the plot haven't quite been plugged yet.
Like the dockyards it celebrates, The Last Ship may not be the most efficient of operations, but there's no doubting the heart behind it.
Change, however, is not the same as betterment, and it is not yet enough of either.
The Last Ship has the rigging of a seaworthy musical, but it inevitably sinks under an hour of dead weight, and perhaps too many yes-men.
The Last Ship is big, overblown, and at times very pretentious – the well-known Geordie sense of humour has gone walkabout.
Sting's political and folk-informed musical masterpiece 'The Last Ship'
There is no denying the power of a story told with an equal mixture of grit and elegance.
It is a real treat to have a musical in which so many of the songs are memorable, melodic and rooted in the world of the story.

This musical is technically superb, with vast sets and projections by 59 Studio, clever lighting (Adam Bassett) and effects, and a real appreciation of the grit and grime of the industry that runs through the blood of those born into it.

Indeed, it is in the design and creative choices where The Last Ship sets sail best, with its superb, expansive design supported by brilliant songs composed and written by Sting himself that seize the essence of the story, its people, and their desperation to survive with terrific vigour.
Musically, this production of The Last Ship is its strongest yet.
The performances, design, company and musicianship all operate at a four-star level.
It is a voyage worth taking, and it manages to stay afloat even if the waters get a little choppy along the way.
The show looks and sounds incredible, making the almost 3-hour runtime enjoyable even if the story itself isn’t always as compelling.
I think the key word to use here is “uneven” as the musical demonstrates some incredible aspects - when it’s good, it’s pretty damn good.
Yet for all its scale, The Last Ship never quite becomes the theatrical powerhouse it ought to be.
This show is clearly full of heart, not just Sting's but the entire cast's, whose talent and attack I applaud for bringing this clunkily-written show to life.
The main issue throughout is simply that there are too many songs, they go on for far too long, and they are staged far too statically.
But when a piece of virtual set is the best thing about a show, you know there’s something wrong.
The Last Ship can’t stay afloat, let alone make port.
Many a dropped jaw will be picked up from the floor by the ushers after the show’s dramatic and panoramic climax.
The musical is engaging and visually beautiful with some fine vocal work and moving lyrics.
Then that ship finally launches, the vast stage comes alive, and for a few spectacular minutes The Last Ship becomes every bit as epic as its title suggests.
Just not quite the triumphant West End premiere this ship deserved.

cn.t: Sting's passion project about Tyneside shipbuilders earns mixed reviews, with critics praising his charismatic performance and soaring score but finding the book ponderous and overlong, leaving a great musical frustratingly out of reach.
